name: Handstand
summary: Wall → freestanding balance (skill, near-daily), then HSPU and press-to-handstand strength tracks.

goal.notes: Freestanding handstand hold; HSPU/press are parallel elite goals

programming.notes: Balance rewards frequency over intensity. HSPU/press are strength days.

safety.notes: Clear kick-up space. Spot or soft landing early on.

divergence_notes: Press vs HSPU first is athlete-dependent — both tracks are valid after freestanding consolidation.

timeline.from_level: 30s freestanding handstand plus a straddle pancake fold
timeline.notes: Gated by compression and pancake range at least as much as by strength. Athletes without mob-pancake progress typically sit at the top of this band indefinitely.

timeline.from_level: 30s chest-to-wall plank, 10 pike push-ups, 30s hollow hold, pain-free 90° wrist extension
timeline.human_label: 9–20 months to a consistent freestanding handstand; a first reliable 10-second freestanding hold typically lands 3–6 months in
timeline.notes: Balance and HSPU tracks run in parallel; the tree total follows the balance track. Sources disagree on the tail — see divergence_notes on the generated tree. Frequency dominates: short daily exposure beats long weekly sessions because this is a motor-learning problem, not a strength problem.

variance_drivers.note: Straight-arm and pulling skills scale roughly with bodyweight at a fixed height. Athletes above ~85 kg routinely sit at the top of every band; lighter athletes at the bottom. This is the single largest driver on lever and planche trees.

Rate of adaptation is logarithmic. An athlete with 3+ years of consistent resistance training moves through early steps in a fraction of the listed time but gains little advantage on the last two steps of any tree.
Connective tissue remodels more slowly with age. Athletes over ~40 should read the upper half of every band and extend tendon-conditioning steps rather than compressing them.
Longer arms and legs lengthen the lever at a fixed bodyweight. Taller athletes commonly need one extra intermediate shape (one-leg before straddle) that shorter athletes can skip.
Below roughly 2 quality sessions per week most athletes stall indefinitely on advanced steps. Gains from going beyond 4–5 sessions per week are small and injury risk rises (arampatzis-2024-loading).
Video review or a coach correcting shape is repeatedly reported to roughly halve time-to-skill on balance-dominant work versus unguided practice (kyleweiger-handstand).
Gymnastics, dance, cheer or yoga backgrounds routinely cut the freestanding milestones to a third of the listed time. This is the strongest single predictor on this tree.

Wrist pain, not balance or strength, is the most commonly reported reason handstand practice stalls. Athletes who skip mob-wrist-load lose more time to forced rest than the conditioning would have cost.

prerequisite_standards.name: Pike push-ups
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Overhead pressing capacity so the shoulders are not the limiter while balancing.

prerequisite_standards.name: Hollow body hold
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Without a hollow the line banana-backs and balance corrections stop working.

prerequisite_standards.name: Loaded wrist extension
prerequisite_standards.rationale: Wrist tolerance is the most frequently reported reason handstand practice stalls.

plateau_signatures.signal: Comfortable for 60s at the wall but under 5s freestanding, for months
typical_causes: All practice volume happening against the wall, which trains the shape but never the correction
No bail-out skill, so the athlete never truly commits
Practising only when fresh enough to be afraid of falling
resolution: Shift at least half the volume to freestanding attempts even though they are short
Drill pirouette and cartwheel exits until falling is boring
Count total freestanding attempts per week as the metric, not hold time

plateau_signatures.signal: Sessions consistently end because of wrist discomfort rather than fatigue or loss of balance
typical_causes: Too much volume added in one jump
resolution: Use parallettes for part of the volume to reduce the extension angle

plateau_signatures.signal: Balance markedly worse after long or frequent sessions, and worse again the following day
typical_causes: Treating a motor-learning skill like a strength session
Practising deep into fatigue, which encodes the wrong corrections
resolution: Cap sessions at 15–20 minutes and raise frequency instead
Stop the session when hold quality drops rather than when time runs out

regression_triggers.trigger: Layoff or markedly reduced training for less than 4 weeks (illness, travel, work crunch)
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: No step lost. Hold times commonly return 10–25% short for the first two sessions; eccentric control and shape quality degrade before maximal strength does.
regression_triggers.action: Resume one step below your unlock for two sessions, then retest. Do not re-earn the whole step — strength-trained athletes show only limited decline at this timescale.

regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Force production falls roughly 7–12%, which usually costs one step on hold-based progressions and one to two steps on the hardest dynamic ones. Recently acquired gains are retained far better than the loss in maximal force suggests.
regression_triggers.action: Restart two steps below your previous unlock and rebuild with full volume but reduced intensity. Expect to regain the lost steps in a fraction of the time they originally took.

regression_triggers.trigger: Planned deload, or four consecutive weeks with no measurable progress
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: None. Hold times often improve in the week after the deload.
regression_triggers.action: Cut volume roughly in half and keep intensity, for one week. Overcoming Gravity's rule is that four weeks without progress means the cycle is finished, not that you need to try harder.

regression_triggers.trigger: Tendon pain forcing modified or stopped training
regression_triggers.typical_dropback: Highly variable. Time lost is usually 6–12 weeks because the tissue must be reloaded from a low baseline, and the affected step is typically lost entirely.
regression_triggers.action: Drop to the last pain-free step, reintroduce isometric then slow eccentric loading, and rebuild across at least 8–12 weeks — the window in which tendon stiffness actually changes. Returning at the previous intensity is the most common cause of recurrence.

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Full bodyweight through ~90° of wrist extension, repeated, with volume rising faster than tissue tolerance
prophylaxis: Non-negotiable wrist prep every session before inverting
Build loaded wrist tolerance over at least 8 weeks before high-volume handstand work
Split volume between floor and parallettes

injury_risk_timeline.mechanism: Repeated end-range overhead pressing at bodyweight before overhead range is fully owned
prophylaxis: Earn overhead flexion without rib flare before HSPU volume
Keep HSPU and balance work on separate days when volume is high
red_flags: Pinching at the top of the press
Loss of overhead range between sessions

productive.notes: The exception to the portfolio-wide 3–4 session default. Balance is a motor-learning problem: many short exposures beat few long ones. Keep sessions to 15–25 minutes and stop on quality, not on the clock.

too_much_signals: Balance clearly worse at the end of a session than at the start, repeatedly
Wrists dictating when the session ends
Kick-ups becoming less consistent week over week
Shoulders sore before the session begins

deload.protocol: Keep frequency, halve the sets, stay at the wall for a week.
deload.trigger: Consistency dropping for two consecutive weeks, or any wrist ache carrying between sessions.
